greeting.text: There is no stall. Tobin, a dragonborn with dull brass scales, sits on a crate at the west milestone. Everything he owns is packed into two panniers. "Buying," he says. "Not selling. Not for a while."

"Mara's lantern." Tobin lifts it from under the counter before you finish. "She sent you. She always sends somebody. Tell her it wasn't lost, just kept somewhere dry." He sets it in front of you, shutter dented and brand up.

"Forty gold clear," Tobin says. "And a history." He lays out the mace-heads carefully. "My name's in the quay book now, one line under eleven consignments I had nothing to do with. Anyone who reads from the top will see a pattern, then find me at the bottom, having signed for it."

"Nineteen days for Reed to write to Greyhythe and learn the man was real, lived at a real address, and has been dead two years," Tobin says. He sets down what he's holding. "I've been in trade thirty-one years. A dead man's name on a live consignment isn't a mistake or a fraud. Nobody's lost anything. It's a *convenience*. Someone wanted goods brought to town that belonged to nobody here."

"They came for it on the fifth night," Tobin says. "Two men, a handcart. No papers, no hurry." He weighs a mace-head without looking at it. "So it was never mine, and it wasn't a trick. Someone needed twelve hundredweight of salt to sit on a public quay for four days under another name. I've spent a fortnight trying to think of an innocent reason."

Tobin reads the bill of lading twice and the copied page of the quay book three times. He sets both on the crate, then sits down beside them. You've never seen him do that.

"Eleven," he says. "Eleven consignments to a man nobody's met. The twelfth has my name on the invoice." He looks up. "Three choices. I pay and sell the salt, and I'm the man who received it. I refuse it, and we see who comes to collect. Or I take it to Reed, and it becomes the town's problem, slowly and in writing, over about a month."

choices.label: Refuse it. Let's see who collects.

greeting.text: "River stair," Tobin says, pointing a claw at the door. "Four crates under a tarpaulin. A porter called Wenn has been sitting beside them for three days, looking professionally uncomfortable. Go look at the paper. I've looked at it, and I'd like a second opinion."

Tobin stands in front of the crate, not behind it. The door is half open behind you before you speak. "I can't," he says. "Before you ask. My carriage came up from Greyhythe this morning with a line on the manifest about who I may sell to. There's no law behind it, and there doesn't need to be." The brass along his jaw has dulled. "Thirty-one years in trade, and nobody's ever told me who my customers can be. Now a clerk is telling me politely, in writing."

"Best month I've had in four years, and I feel wretched about every coin of it," Tobin says as he lays out mace-heads. "Carters are coming through in numbers. The road's clear, and half of them want to see the quarry on the way past. I've started selling them lanterns."

Tobin's added a new line of goods and looks pleased. "Quarry stone. Dressed, cheap, delivered to the east gate on market day by a goblin with a slate who corrects my arithmetic." He gives a great shrug. "Half my regulars won't come to the stall now. The other half have doubled their orders. Net, I'm up."
"The Hallowmere wagon," Tobin says, pointing a claw at you. "You got it through the cut. Two of my crates were on it. Take ten off anything on this table, and don't argue with me."

"The northern ford," Tobin says without enthusiasm. "Yes. Nothing's been raided, but it's nine miles longer. I've lost the two carters who wouldn't ride an extra nine miles for what I pay." He sets out the mace-heads. "Safe isn't the same as good. Nobody here wants to hear that."
"Arms, armour, and potions. Fair prices, no questions." The half-dragonborn doesn't look up from his crate. "That last part's advertising. I ask plenty of questions. I just don't act on the answers."

choices.label: You have been staring at that invoice since I came in.

the_invoice.text:
"I've been staring at it since Tuesday." Tobin turns the paper so you can see it. "Twelve hundredweight of coarse salt, landed at the river stair, carriage paid, invoiced to me. I didn't order it. I can't prove I didn't, because a man can't prove what he hasn't done. That's not a legal problem. It's how the world works."

He taps the page with one claw.

"And here's what's kept me up. It's *good salt*. I could sell it all within a fortnight and make a profit. Nobody tricks a man by giving him something he can sell."

interjections.text: Sera: "Then it is not a trick on you. You are somewhere for it to be, that is all."

choices.label: I'll go and look at it.
Then pay it and sell the salt.
That is between you and the quay.

he_is_relieved.text: "Thank you," Tobin says, brisk with relief. "River stair. The porter's Wenn. Big, cheerful, can't read a word, remembers everything. I'd pay for that combination if I could find it twice. Check the bill, then the quay book."

not_that_simple.text: "It's exactly that simple, and that's the trouble," Tobin says. "The moment I pay the carriage, I've received the consignment. In writing, in the quay book. Whatever it was for, I'm now the man it was sent to." He gives a great shrug. "I've been in trade thirty-one years. A thing that costs nothing and makes you a profit is the only thing worth fearing."

choices.label: All right. I'll go and look at it.

pays_and_keeps.text:
He pays the carriage and signs for the salt. It sells within a fortnight, though not at a price he's comfortable with.

"Forty gold clear," says Tobin Brassscale, counting sixty of it into your hand for the trouble, "and one line in a public book, in my own hand, right under eleven consignments belonging to a man nobody's ever met."

He shuts the drawer.

"I've made money," he says, "and picked up a history. I've done that before, in two other towns, and both times it took about four years to find out what the history was for."

choices.label: Can you take your name off the quay book?

refuses_it.text:
He formally refuses the crates in front of the quay master. They sit on the landing for four days, unclaimed.

On the fifth night, two men come up the stair with a handcart. They show no papers and argue with no one. They walk straight to the right crates, load them, and take them downriver. It takes nine minutes.

Mott Wenn watches and doesn't stop them. Nobody's ever told him to stop anyone, and the men look like they're doing an ordinary job.

interjections.text: Kessa, from the dark at the top of the steps: "Nine minutes. They've done that before."
Ilse: "They knew which crates in the dark. Somebody told them where it would be stacked."

choices.label: Say nothing and let them go.

to_the_captain.text:
Reed takes the bill of lading, reads it twice, and writes to Greyhythe that afternoon. That's faster than most things happen in town.

The answer comes back in nineteen days. The consignee was a real man with a real address in Greyhythe. He's been dead two years, and his estate is still open.

Reed dates the answer and writes it in the day book herself. Then she puts down the pen and says, to no one in particular, that Rivermark law has no offence for a dead man receiving salt.

interjections.text: Aldric: "She has written it down. That is not nothing. It is very nearly nothing, and it is not nothing."

cannot_unsign.text: "You can't unsign the quay book," Tobin says. "That's the point of a quay book." He returns to the crate. "I'll do what I've always done and keep excellent records of my own. When someone comes asking, I'll have the better book. It has worked twice. I wouldn't call it a plan."

convenient_for_what.text:
"For arriving," Tobin says. "Salt, lime, oil, rope, boards. Those aren't just goods. They're a *list*, the sort of things a man buys to keep something dry, light something, and hold something up." He spreads his claws. "Every one landed in Rivermark. None belonged to anyone here, and none is still on the quay."

He pauses.

"I sell rope. Nobody bought theirs from me."

no_innocent_reason.text:
"No luck," Tobin says. "I've been generous with myself about it. The alternative's unpleasant." He sets down the mace-head. "Best I can figure, someone wanted goods on a public quay under a name nobody could question, then planned to take them somewhere they couldn't pass through a gate."

He looks at you.

"That's not a crime, or even unusual. I've done something like it over a customs matter and slept fine. But twelve consignments isn't a customs matter." He picks up the mace-head again.

the_rumours.text: Tobin lowers his voice, which for him is still audible across a market. "Nobody has called a council since the quarry. Reed signs things and they happen and it is, I will be honest with you, extremely convenient." He weighs a mace-head. "I have been in three towns where that was extremely convenient. I left all three."

"You have been to the granary." Tobin does not look up. "Everybody who has been to the granary has the same face afterwards. He is charming, he is entirely reasonable, and you come away having agreed to something." A pause. "He holds my winter credit. I want that said out loud so that you know what my opinion is worth."

choices.label: What does he hold over you?

the_rumours.text: "The Vance girl keeps the mill's books and has done since she was twenty-one," Tobin says. "Alone. Nobody checks. I have said that to two watch captains and one of them wrote it down." He shrugs. "That is the whole of my contribution to public life."

"Spoiled grain in Hearthstone's cellar," Tobin repeats, and puts down what he is holding. "With a tally on it. With a *stamp* on it." He looks at you with real, unhappy respect. "You want to be careful who you show that to and in what order."

"Goblins in the quarry, gnolls on the road, and the price of salt." Tobin ticks them off. "Those are the three subjects. There has not been a fourth in this town since the mill roof." He looks up. "There is a warden works the east hills. Thornwood. She has a fourth subject and nobody will sit still for it."

the_credit.text: "Two hundred and forty gold, rolled every winter for six years," Tobin says. "He has never once called it in and he has never once let me forget he could." He goes back to the crate. "That is not a complaint. It is a very good business arrangement. It is simply also a leash, and I would rather you heard me say the word than worked it out later and wondered."

no_use_for_that.text: "Nor am I, particularly," Tobin says. "I have my stock, I have my scales, and I have a road west. That is more than most of them got out with." He looks back once, at the smoke line. "Do not travel with me. I mean that pleasantly."

he_will_not_risk_it.text: "No," Tobin says, and the word costs him. "They wouldn't come to me. They'd go after the carriage. That's four men with families in Greyhythe, and nobody would explain it to them. The price would just rise and stay there." He opens the door the rest of the way. "When things change, come back. I'll sell you this whole table at cost, gladly. It is not going to change this month."
